7.0.0.en: 1 My son, keep my words, and lay up my commandments with thee. 2 Keep my commandments, and live; and my law as the apple of thine eye. 3 Bind them upon thy fingers, write them upon the table of thine heart. 4 Say unto wisdom, Thou art my sister; and call understanding thy kinswoman: 5 That they may keep thee from the strange woman, from the stranger which flattereth with her words.

7.0.1.en: As is his custom, the wise Solomon calls us to listen to the voice of the commandment and to concentrate on it, for the divine commandment presented to us by our fathers and guides is more precious than all the treasures of the earth. Its blessings are as follows:

7.0.2.en: First: a source of life. "My son, keep my words, and lay up my commandments with thee."

7.0.3.en: By saying "Keep... lay up my commandments," he affirms that we must be occupied with the Holy Bible, not to be read hastily, but to be stored in the depths of the heart, so that the word of God becomes daily nourishment for the soul and an inseparable part of our life.

7.0.5.en: The divine commandments are spirit and life (Jn 6:23); they raise the soul from death to give it the new life in Christ Jesus. They transform the carnal man into a spiritual man, that he may enjoy the spiritual body instead of the natural (1 Cor 2:14) and enter into the Kingdom of God, which flesh and blood cannot inherit (1 Cor 15:50). This is accomplished by the commandment, which presents to him the person of "the divine Word." For the commandment is not merely an order for excellent moral conduct or a prohibition of vice, but a living encounter with the person of the Lord Christ, the Word of God, who said: "I am the life," and "I am the resurrection." Without Him the soul remains in the tomb of sin, bearing the odor of corruption, until it hears the divine voice: "Lazarus, come forth," and the Lord commands His disciples (His priests) to loose its bands, and the soul enjoys the new life.

7.0.6.en: When we open the door of the heart to the Lord Christ, the word of God who gives life, He dwells in us, and sin flees and cannot remain.

7.0.7.en: The commandment of the Gospel is the axis of the life of every Christian. Therefore, when St. John Cassian spoke in his book the Institutes about the monastic life in Egypt as an ideal Christian life, he called monasticism an evangelical or Christian life that revolves around the Gospel of the Lord Christ.

7.0.8.en: Bishop Ignatius Brianchaninov says: [The holy monks of old call the monastic life a life according to the commandments of the Gospel. St. John Climacus defines the monk thus: "A monk is one who is led by the commandments of God alone, the word of God, at all times, in every place, and in every matter." The monks under St. Pachomius the Great were bound to keep the Gospel by heart, so that it might always be before the eyes of the mind and be imprinted on the soul, so that it might fulfill it easily and successfully. The blessed Elder Seraphim said: "We must thus train ourselves that our mind may meditate on the law of the Lord, which becomes the leader of our life and the regulator of it"... The Holy Spirit teaches and leads the true servants of God who have become His.]

7.1.0.en: Second: a source of light and spiritual insight. "Keep... my law as the apple of thine eye" [2].

7.1.1.en: It is the inner insight, by which we look to see God in His glory, and perceive heaven with all its hosts, and by which we have a sound view of mankind and all creation, as of the body and temporal life. If the commandment is broken we remain in darkness and lose sight. If the eye is very precious in a person's life, its pupil is the most precious thing a person cherishes. The word "pupil" came in Hebrew to mean a very tiny man, a "mini man." So the text would be: "my law as a little man in thine eye." When a person draws near to look into another person's eyes, he sees his own image imprinted on them. Here the father advises his son to draw very near to the commandment, so that the image of the commandment may be imprinted on his eyes, and the commandment shine forth in them, so that he sees everything through the commandment. The same expression is used in (Deut 32:10; Ps 17:8).

7.1.2.en: Origen sees in the Lord Christ's address to the holy soul, His bride: "Thou hast doves' eyes" (Song 4:2), an indication of her nearness and cleaving to the Holy Spirit, so that His image appears imprinted on the pupils of her eyes, to see everything through the Holy Spirit.

7.1.3.en: Concerning this expression it is said: "The eyeball, and in its center the pupil, has been called the apple because its shape is round. Because of its great value and for the sake of its strict protection, the two eyelids surrounding it close automatically when there is the slightest possibility of danger; therefore it has become a symbol of what is very precious and must be guarded with care. So it is fitting for us to take care of the commandment and surround it with our whole being, lest we break it and be exposed to spiritual blindness. It seems very small like the pupil of the eye, but it is exceedingly precious: without it we do not see the open gates of heaven, and at the same time it can easily suffer grave damage."

7.2.0.en: Third: a support for worship and work. "Bind them upon thy fingers" [3]

7.2.1.en: Thus whenever you lift up your arms in prayer you speak with God through His commandment, which is full of divine promises. And if you stretch out your hands to work, you do everything through it, so that your work is holy. The commandment is bound about the neck as an indication of the mark of kingship and the surpassing honor that we receive through it, and it is bound on the fingers to support us in our prayers and our practical conduct.

7.2.2.en: Some of the Jews were accustomed to put some texts of the Holy Bible in a leather case and bind it on their foreheads or their arms during prayer. The leather case was bound around the left arm with seven straps, and then the strap was wound seven times around the middle finger.

7.2.3.en: Some think that binding them on the fingers is realized in many ways, among them engraving them on rings. Kings and great men used to engrave their names on rings, and when the king trusted a person he gave him his ring to seal every royal command with it. So in place of our names we engrave the commandment of God on the fingers, to seal our thoughts, our words, our deeds and our prayers with the seal of the commandment, so that they carry heavenly power.

7.3.0.en: Fourth: preserving feelings and emotions. "Write them upon the table of thine heart" [3]

7.3.1.en: It is not enough to bind the commandment on the arm and the finger; it must be bound to the heart. It establishes the Kingdom of God within you, and so preserves and sanctifies every emotion, feeling and sensation, and all your works come forth from a heart pure and faithful to God. Thus the commandment is bound to our whole inner being and is not merely an outward ornament in which we take pride before men.

7.3.2.en: Fifth: entering into a relationship of kinship. "Say unto wisdom, Thou art my sister; and call understanding thy kinswoman" [4].

7.3.3.en: Although the book of Proverbs is concerned with the fitting and wise conduct of the believer in all aspects of his life, yet through its lines it brings the believer into the encounter with "the incarnate Wisdom of God," so that the soul may accept union with Him and share His nature, and practice the new, risen life. It is occupied with the Bridegroom dwelling in its depths and converses with Him in a spirit of love and joy. Thus its conduct changes, not in its outward appearance only, but in its hidden roots.

7.3.4.en: Through wisdom we are made worthy to belong to the heavenly family, and so we count our Christ as the firstborn Brother, who is the Creator, the Savior and the Almighty and wise Lord. When the soul calls to wisdom: "My sister, my kinswoman," it bears a kind of respect for wisdom together with intense nearness to her, and enters with her into a kinship resembling "blood kinship," and has a special boldness before her.

7.3.5.en: The calling of wisdom "my sister" points to a marital union, for the word brother or sister is sometimes used for a husband or wife (Gen 20:2, 12; 26:7; Song 4:9, 10, 12; 5:1, 2). If adultery comes to a person as a woman who wishes to unite with him to satisfy his fleshly lusts, Wisdom truly comes forward as the Bridegroom of the soul, uniting with her eternally, to satisfy all her needs on a joyful heavenly level, so that the believer lacks nothing! When Wisdom came incarnate, many adulterers and tax collectors gathered around Him, who truly found what satisfied their inner depths, and left corruption, not by compulsion, nor in repression, but with a true joy that cannot be expressed!

7.3.6.en: The personification of Wisdom here is important, for it prepares the way for (chapters 8 and 9), where Wisdom comes forward as a being who invites us to her own banquet, which is the banquet of the eternal wedding.

7.4.0.en: Sixth: protection from the deceit of evil. "That they may keep thee from the strange woman, from the stranger which flattereth with her words" [5].

7.4.1.en: After presenting the commandment in its positive work, where it gives the soul life, enlightenment, true worship and holy work, and preserves and sanctifies feelings and emotions, and brings us into belonging to heaven, it also, on the negative side, keeps us from the deceits of the evil enemy, especially through the words of the flattering adulteress. It alone is able to protect us from the shame of defiled relationships with a wicked strange woman. For none will keep a man from the folly of the adulteress except the Lady (Wisdom).

7.5.s.en: 2. Warning against the wiles of the adulteress

7.5.0.en: 6 For at the window of my house I looked through my casement, 7 And beheld among the simple ones, I discerned among the youths, a young man void of understanding, 8 Passing through the street near her corner; and he went the way to her house, 9 In the twilight, in the evening, in the black and dark night: 10 And, behold, there met him a woman with the attire of an harlot, and subtil of heart. 11 (She is loud and stubborn; her feet abide not in her house: 12 Now is she without, now in the streets, and lieth in wait at every corner.) 13 So she caught him, and kissed him, and with an impudent face said unto him, 14 I have peace offerings with me; this day have I payed my vows. 15 Therefore came I forth to meet thee, diligently to seek thy face, and I have found thee. 16 I have decked my bed with coverings of tapestry, with carved works, with fine linen of Egypt. 17 I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon. 18 Come, let us take our fill of love until the morning: let us solace ourselves with loves. 19 For the goodman is not at home, he is gone a long journey: 20 He hath taken a bag of money with him, and will come home at the day of the new moon.

7.5.1.en: Since the wise Solomon tasted the bitterness of marriage to pagan women, and his feet slipped into the worship of their pagan gods, he was therefore occupied in this book with the good wife, for he closed it with the most wonderful song in which he praises the good wife. And in order to reveal her importance, he spoke in the body of the book of three kinds of wicked wives, to prepare for this song by presenting the negatives first. These three kinds, the opposite of the good wife, are:

7.5.4.en: * The woman beautiful in form but without wisdom or discretion (Prov 11:22).

7.5.5.en: The wise Solomon presents to us a tragic story in which he declares the role of the adulterous woman as she snares a foolish young man in her trap. In this story the wise man appears himself as an eyewitness of an event he watched through the window of his house, when he saw a foolish young man void of understanding hunted by a married woman who seduces him to commit sin. What he saw is an example among countless numbers of simple ones who fall every day into the deceit of evil.

7.5.6.en: He says: "For at the window of my house I looked through my casement" [6]. The wise man speaks as an eyewitness, presenting a practical, realistic account. The wise man himself looks out secretly to see the tragic scene of the unfaithful wife who plays the part of a harlot hunting the simple. Perhaps by this scene he reminds us of what was carved on pieces of ivory in many regions of Phoenicia, namely the goddess Ashtoreth looking out of the window. Her worship was linked with adultery, as priestesses devoted themselves to this work in the pagan temples. What a difference between the wise man who looks out in bitterness in order to cry out, guide and rescue, and the goddess who looks out to find her pleasure in the corruption of people's lives and their eternal perdition.

7.5.7.en: The wise man describes the young man who fell into the cords of this adulteress as follows:

7.6.0.en: First: "void of understanding" [7], that is, he has trivial thinking; wisdom has no place in his depths, and he does not seek it with any seriousness.

7.7.0.en: Second: "passing through the street" [8]; he has no serious aim in his life, but passes along the road wandering idly, occupied with nothing important in his life. Perhaps this trait is among the most dangerous, that a person be empty of mind and heart and without work, like one who loiters in the streets without aim. As St. John Cassian says: "He who works is attacked by one demon, but he who does not work is attacked by all the demons."

7.7.1.en: Third: "Passing... near her corner, and he went the way to her house" [8]. He does not guard against falling, nor does he flee from danger; he is like one who drives his car through a red light.

7.7.2.en: We can say that he missed the way, for his inner lusts drew him toward the place of sin. We do not blame the sinful woman as much as we blame the young man who went to her door to meet her so that she seduced him. Sin lay hidden in his heart, so he responded to the call of the evil outside.

7.8.0.en: Fourth: he walks "in the twilight, in the evening, in the black and dark night" [9]. He does not know the light, nor walk by day, nor enjoy the rays of the Sun of Righteousness. He also walks outside the circle of Christ, where there is darkness of heart and mind. Verse 9 contains five Hebrew words, all of which mean "darkness," to affirm that the adulteress does not bring the one she snares only to the end of his day, but into the very darkness. For if the adulteress has submitted to the authority of "the prince of darkness," she finds her pleasure in capturing others with her, so that all may live with her in the humiliation of darkness. It is said in the Gospel according to our teacher John the Beloved: "Men loved darkness rather than light, because their deeds were evil" (Jn 3:19), "I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life" (Jn 8:12).

7.8.1.en: The wise man presents to us an exact description of a woman who incites a young man to sin, her lust inflamed:

7.9.0.en: First: she wears "the attire of an harlot" [10], to stir up thoughts in those around her inclined toward evil. She is married, but with boldness, without modesty or shame, she seeks evil, and uses all the methods of the world to entice.

7.9.1.en: Second: "subtil of heart" [10]; what she says and how she behaves differ from what she harbors in her depths. No sign of divine grace appears on her.

7.10.0.en: Third: "She is loud and stubborn" [11]. She does not have the grace of inner quiet or balance in her conduct, but is full of clamor and noise. She knows no inner rest; however many sweet words she offers or however cheerful her face, she is always in a state of anxiety and clamor. As Isaiah the prophet says: "There is no peace, saith the LORD, unto the wicked" (Isa 48:22; 57:21). She is also obstinate, hard-headed and violent, and knows no control of her feelings and conduct. As it is said: "Israel slideth back as a backsliding heifer" (Hos 4:16).

7.10.1.en: Fourth: "her feet abide not in her house" [11], for she finds her pleasure in the streets and public squares, not in her house, contrary to what the Apostle Paul advises the young women, saying: "To love their husbands, to love their children, to be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed" (Titus 2:4, 5).

7.11.0.en: She does not stay in her house, but runs in the streets to set her nets and hunt the simple and the foolish. "Now is she without, now in the streets, and lieth in wait at every corner" [12]. Sin is very easy to come by; it throws itself upon every person in order to attract him. The wise man portrays the adulteress as having a house, not a home; she has a building but not a family that enjoys its warmth, and she does not shed on them her love and care. She may have a husband and children, but they have no place in her heart, nor in her thoughts. She finds her pleasure in going out of her house to set her nets and hunt the simple. Therefore the Apostle advises the young women to be "chaste, keepers at home, good" (Titus 2:5).

7.12.0.en: Fifth: she bears the image of love and gentleness in her dealings: "So she caught him, and kissed him" [13]. She embraces him with her arms and kisses him with her mouth, and the young man thinks he is happy and has found what satisfies him, and does not realize that she offers him lust, not love.

7.12.1.en: Sixth: she bears the image of religiosity.

7.12.2.en: "With an impudent face said unto him:

7.12.3.en: I have peace offerings with me; this day have I payed my vows. Therefore came I forth to meet thee, diligently to seek thy face, and I have found thee" [13-15].

7.12.4.en: She pretends to be religious, offering peace offerings, which are voluntary sacrifices (Lev 7), and she invites him to share with her in a religious meal. Thus he thinks that he has not sinned, for he has found one who is religious, and who offers him love along with the food. She snares him by deceit and draws him through his belly.

7.12.5.en: * When the stomach is filled with all kinds of food, the seeds of lust are generated, and the mind, when it is weighed down with food, cannot keep the control of its thoughts. For the mind is made drunk not only by wine but also by the abundance of kinds of food, which weaken it and rob it of all its power and capacity for pure, clean contemplation.

7.12.6.en: St. John Cassian * Just as the ear of purity is the product of the seed of sweat in fasting, so excessive fullness causes dissolution and excess produces defilement. But if the belly is left hungry and humbled, shameful thoughts will not rush into the soul.

7.12.7.en: St. Isaac the Syrian Perhaps she wanted to express to him how much she cared for him: she made a vow to God for his sake that He might give him health and safety, and now she invites him to share in this special banquet of the vow. She is more occupied with his health and peace than with herself!

7.12.8.en: We often fall into troubles because of our concentration on outward appearances, so that we wear the mask of religiosity to hide a corrupt heart, or as St. Augustine says, that we find in the Church some who wear sheep's clothing, but inside them are the hearts of ravening wolves. When a king was being chosen according to God's heart, the Lord said to Samuel: "Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature... for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart" (1 Sam 16:7).

7.12.9.en: If the wicked woman hunts the young man by the deceptive outward appearance, the young man surrenders himself to adultery not only through his laxity with the causes of sin, but also through his arrogance and love of vainglory.

7.12.10.en: * Vainglory is the servant of adultery.

7.12.11.en: * The man who boasts of his practice of virtue is allowed to fall into adultery. And he who is full of imaginations because of his wisdom is allowed to fall into the dark nets of ignorance.

7.12.12.en: St. Isaac the Syrian Some interpret this verse as meaning that the woman seduces the young man by being ceremonially clean, so that she thinks that whoever clings to her in bodily relations is not defiled, although this opinion is not acceptable. Others see that she makes clear to him that she is clean from "the monthly sickness." For whoever lies with a woman in her menstruation is unclean seven days (Lev 15:24). Or perhaps she makes clear to him that he may be joined to her without fear, since she is not exposed to pregnancy. In any case, she links adultery with worship, which was known among the Phoenicians in their worship of the goddess Ashtoreth, and the Law warned against this. Also by her saying: "this day have I payed my vows" she means that she has offered peace offerings, and according to the Law she may eat from the sacrifice on the day on which the sacrifice was offered and the day after. It is as though she says to him: "I have an abundance of delicious food for us to enjoy." Thus she draws him by the lust of his belly. For she knows that she can hunt his heart through his stomach.

7.12.13.en: She pretends that she came out to seek his face, and did not cease searching until she found him! These are words of deceit, for she is not seeking a particular person but seeking what is for herself, to satisfy her emotions or instincts, and in his folly the one who has fallen a victim in her hands thinks that he is the very important person sought by her. She confuses his concepts so that he does not distinguish between love and lust.

7.12.14.en: Seventh: she invites him to enjoy a marital night.

7.12.15.en: "I have decked my bed with coverings of tapestry, with carved works, with fine linen of Egypt.

7.12.16.en: I have perfumed my bed with myrrh, aloes, and cinnamon.

7.12.17.en: Come, let us take our fill of love until the morning.

7.13.0.en: Let us solace ourselves with loves" [16-18].

7.13.1.en: Besides her moral dissolution and the inflaming of her fleshly lusts, this woman is marked by betrayal of her husband and unfaithfulness.

7.13.2.en: She uses every sensory means to attract this foolish young man: the luxurious, soft bed, the precious linen, and the alluring perfumes. She wants to attract him with all the senses: he sees the provocative clothes and the bed spread with coverings of tapestry, and hears the sound of her invitation since she sought him and searched for him until she found him, and feels her affection until morning, and tastes the sweetness of her lips, and smells the perfumes. Thus sin enters us through the five senses, therefore the Holy Bible is concerned with sanctifying these senses, not destroying them, but raising and directing them to be satisfied with what is for building, not tearing down.

7.13.3.en: Sadly she invites the young man to sin with her on her bed, which she shares with her husband, and so offers him what belongs to her bridegroom for the account of evil. We offer the heart to the kingdom of darkness instead of the kingdom of light, and turn our mind into a stage for evil instead of the manifestation of heaven in it, and squander our emotions, feelings and sensations instead of sanctifying them.

7.13.4.en: Eighth: the circumstances are prepared for the pleasure of love; nothing lacks for them except his consent and response to her.

7.13.5.en: "For the goodman is not at home.

7.13.6.en: He is gone a long journey.

7.13.7.en: He hath taken a bag of money with him.

7.14.0.en: And will come home at the day of the new moon" [19-20].

7.14.1.en: It is as though she invites him to spend the night with her without fear, for her husband will not return to his house until the appearance of the crescent, or the new month. Is this not the enticement of sin to the soul, so that it brings it in as into a pitch-dark night, and offers it every reassurance as though the Bridegroom of the soul were absent and would not return until the day of judgment!

7.14.2.en: In the same spirit Potiphar's wife called Joseph to sin with her, for her husband was absent, but he believed that the eyes of God were watching him, for he said to her: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" (Gen 39:9).

7.15.s.en: 3. The folly of the one who falls into her nets

7.15.0.en: 21 With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him. 22 He goeth after her straightway, as an ox goeth to the slaughter, or as a fool to the correction of the stocks; 23 Till a dart strike through his liver; as a bird hasteth to the snare, and knoweth not that it is for his life.

7.15.1.en: In folly the young man fell, whom he described as void of understanding [7], trivial in his thinking and walking through life without aim. He became like an ox led to the slaughter, like a fool led to punishment, and like a bird hastening to the snare. He acts without awareness, for the woman drew him with the fetters of his lust without his realizing that the price is his whole life or his soul.

7.15.2.en: "With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him.

7.15.3.en: He goeth after her straightway, as an ox goeth to the slaughter, or as a fool to the correction of the stocks.

7.15.4.en: Till a dart strike through his liver.

7.15.5.en: As a bird hasteth to the snare, and knoweth not that it is for his life" [21-23].

7.15.6.en: Perhaps he means here that the man will come one day and discover what the young man has done, and will strike their liver with the dart and sentence them both to death.

7.15.7.en: And even if the husband does not discover the truth, the two of them will not be able to justify themselves before divine justice, and their portion will be eternal perdition.

7.15.8.en: Adultery is the shortest road to destruction, whether at the hand of the husband who discovers the crime, or because of the venereal diseases under whose weight the adulterer falls, or the mental and psychological confusion, and what is more important, eternal ruin and deprivation of fellowship in the heavenly life.

7.16.0.en: Hearken unto me now therefore, O ye children, and attend to the words of my mouth:

7.16.1.en: Let not thine heart decline to her ways, go not astray in her paths.

7.16.2.en: For she hath cast down many wounded: yea, many strong men have been slain by her. Her house is the way to hell, going down to the chambers of death." [24-27].

7.16.3.en: Truly "many strong men have been slain by her," although we have been given power to overcome her, and those who are with us are more than those who are against us; but by being lax with small things we fall into great ones. Therefore the voice of the Lord to Lot was: "Escape for thy life." The Fathers were concerned with this divine principle.

7.16.4.en: St. Piamun the Great says: "It is good to avoid the causes of sin. The man who approaches the opportunities of sin is like a person sitting on the edge of a cliff; the enemy can hunt him easily whenever he wishes."

7.16.5.en: And St. Isaac the Syrian says: "Our falling into various sins is caused not by the sins in themselves but by our weakness, whereby our nature falls easily. Therefore there is urgent need to beware of them."

7.16.6.en: * Whoever does not withdraw by his own will from the causes of the passions, sin draws him against his will.

7.16.7.en: The causes of sin are wine, (wicked) women, wealth, and excessive concern for the health of the body. These things are not sins by their nature... For this reason it is fitting for a person to be on guard against them with great care.

7.16.8.en: * Beware of small things so that you do not fall into great things.

7.16.9.en: Do not be slack in your work, lest you be put to shame when you stand in the midst of your companions, and be without provisions on your journey, and be alone by the side of the road.

7.16.10.en: St. Isaac the Syrian Who is this unfaithful wife who hunts souls to bring them down to death?!

7.16.11.en: If this chapter can be interpreted literally concerning the falling of young men into the sin of adultery, it can also apply to many sins that present themselves as maidens hunting the soul from its Bridegroom, so that it loses its union with God. If the wise Solomon reveals here the nets of the adulterous woman for hunting the foolish, then all sins set their varied nets in one form or another, especially the deceitful teachers who use every attractive means to corrupt the faith of the simple.

7.16.12.en: Some see that it refers to the apostate churches that bear the name of the Lord Christ but offer false teachings. She betrays her Bridegroom, and does not cease working without interruption to draw souls by every means from the house of the true Church. She carries every philosophical beauty and offers many means of luxury, so that believers leave the narrow way of the cross and enter the broad way which pushes them to eternal perdition.

7.16.13.en: * You have seen how great is the harm of the adulteress!

7.16.14.en: Do not allow lust to rise up, for its death is eternal. As for her words and her sweet speech and her wounds, by her sins she kills those who submit to her. Her evil has many forms that lead to descent into hell. As for "the chambers of death," they mean either death or its storehouses. How then can one escape from it?

7.17.s.en: Then I shall settle in my eternal home!

7.17.0.en: * Let me keep Your commandments as the apple of my eye.

7.17.1.en: It is exceedingly precious; without it I lose sight, and live in darkness!

7.17.2.en: Let me bind it on the fingers of my soul as a unique ring!

7.17.3.en: With it I seal all my thoughts, my words and my deeds.

7.17.4.en: Let it not depart from my eyes, nor be taken away from before me.

7.17.5.en: * Let me carry You within me, O Wisdom of God, and be united with You, O Bridegroom of my soul.

7.17.6.en: You alone satisfy my whole being!

7.17.8.en: Deep within me, You carry me into the depths of Your hidden divine mysteries.

7.17.9.en: And You lift me up to the throne of Your grace.

7.17.10.en: * With You I fly as if to heaven, so the snares of the adulteress will not close upon my feet, nor will my heart fall into her hidden nets.

7.17.11.en: * What do I see in this deceiver?

7.17.12.en: She is a stranger by race.

7.17.13.en: But I have become Your son!

7.17.14.en: She flatters with her words, but You put truth in my mouth.

7.17.15.en: She is an unfaithful adulteress, who knows no faithfulness, but in You I become faithful to the end.

7.17.16.en: She is void of understanding because she resists You, O Wisdom of God; but by Your grace I become wise.

7.17.17.en: She wears the garments of a harlot, glittering and alluring, but I hide myself in You, O my eternal wedding garment.

7.17.18.en: I put You on, and so I bear Your surpassing righteousness!

7.17.19.en: She is loud and finds her pleasure in noise, * but I meet You with calm of soul and stillness of heart.

7.17.20.en: She is exceedingly stubborn and obstinate, but I long to bear Your obedience.

7.17.21.en: In her house her feet abide not, but I see in the heavens an open door.

7.17.22.en: I see You carrying me to the bosom of Your Father; there Your fiery Spirit carries me, and I settle as in my eternal home.

7.17.23.en: * The adulteress roams outside, in the streets, and at every corner.

7.17.24.en: But I enter into the depths, and enjoy my heavenly home.

7.17.25.en: My soul will not roam among the enticements of the world and its passing pleasures.

7.17.26.en: She catches others and kisses them with her mouth, opens her heart like a wolf to devour whoever clings to her.

7.17.27.en: Give me a heart that knows no enmity and bears no hatred, but melts with love even toward those who oppose it.

7.17.28.en: She is deceitful even in the appearances of religiosity, but I cry out to You: remove from me Pharisaism, and give me inner purity of heart!

7.17.29.en: * Yes, whenever I see sin embodied in one form or another, my heart is kindled the more, longing to set out to You, for in You alone my depths find rest.

7.17.30.en: Carry me to Yourself, O desire of my heart!
